learning_objectives: Form simple yes/no questions with familiar present forms of essere and avere.
Choose a basic interrogative word according to the information requested.
Ask and answer short A1 questions with natural Italian word order.
scope_included: chi, che cosa, dove, quando, come, perché, quanto

skills.description_en: Form simple yes/no questions with familiar present-tense clauses and natural Italian word order.
Select chi, che cosa, dove, quando, come, perché or quanto according to the information requested.
Place an interrogative word naturally before a simple clause without English-style auxiliary inversion.
Give short contextual answers to basic yes/no and question-word questions.
Use the correct previously learned present forms of essere and avere inside basic questions.
Produce short natural A1 questions for basic personal and practical information.

lesson.short_explanation_en: Italian basic questions are usually simpler than English ones. A familiar present-tense clause can become a yes/no question without adding do/does and without a required subject–verb inversion: Hai fame? Use an interrogative word when you need one specific piece of information: chi (who), che cosa (what), dove (where), quando (when), come (how / what ... like), perché (why), and quanto (how much/how many). Keep the verb in the form required by its subject. In speech, intonation signals a yes/no question; in writing, use a question mark.

rule_blocks.explanation_en: With the simple present forms already learned, Italian does not need an extra auxiliary equivalent to English do/does. A familiar clause can be used directly as a question.
usage_notes_en: Explicit subject pronouns are still usually omitted unless needed for contrast or clarity.
common_errors_en: Do not add an invented equivalent of English do/does.
Do not change sei to è or hai to ha when you are asking tu.

rule_blocks.explanation_en: Choose the interrogative word according to the missing information.
common_errors_en: Use chi for people, not dove.
Use dove for a place and quando for a time.
Use perché when asking for a reason.

rule_blocks.heading_en: Natural word order and short answers
rule_blocks.explanation_en: A question word commonly comes before the simple clause. The finite verb keeps its normal person and number. Answers can be short when the context makes the missing information clear.
usage_notes_en: Italian does not require the English pattern do + subject + verb.
A yes/no answer can begin with sì or no.
common_errors_en: Avoid mechanically copying English do-support: *Dove do...* is not Italian.
Keep agreement: Dove sono i libri?, not *Dove è i libri?*.

rows: Anna è a casa? / Marco ha un cane?

focus_items.explanation_en: A familiar statement pattern can be used as a yes/no question; Italian does not require a separate do-support auxiliary.
The present form sei remains the same inside the question.
Hai keeps its normal second-person singular form in a yes/no question.

contexts.setting_en: In a classroom, simple questions ask for a person, an object, a place, a time and a quantity.
